demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Rajendra "Raj" Patel, an 80-year-old widowed Coast Guard veteran, sat in his favorite armchair, surrounded by the familiar comforts of his home. Yet, despite the tranquility of his surroundings, Raj's mind often wandered back to that fateful day when he accidentally caused a serious injury to one of his crew members during a rescue operation. The incident had left an indelible mark on his psyche, and over time, Raj found himself struggling to come to terms with what had transpired. As he reminisced about the event, Raj's memories came in fragmented pieces – disconnected images and sounds that refused to coalesce into a coherent narrative. He recalled the sound of sirens blaring in the distance, the cries for help from the stranded vessel, and the feeling of panic that gripped him as he realized his mistake. However, whenever he tried to deliberately recall the events leading up to the accident, Raj found himself drawing a blank. The memories seemed to be shrouded in a thick fog, inaccessible and elusive. The aftermath of the incident had been just as distressing for Raj. He began to avoid going to unfamiliar places, fearing that he wouldn't be able to assess potential dangers. Even simple tasks like taking a walk in the park or visiting new restaurants became daunting challenges. Raj's loved ones noticed a change in him – he became increasingly withdrawn and isolated, preferring the safety of his home to the uncertainty of the outside world. Raj also started engaging in magical thinking, telling himself that the event hadn't really happened or that it wasn't as severe as he remembered. He forced himself to focus on positive thoughts, suppressing any negative emotions that threatened to surface. However, these coping mechanisms provided only temporary relief, and Raj soon found himself taking unnecessary risks – a behavior that both frightened and puzzled him. The sounds of sirens still sent shivers down his spine, transporting him back to that fateful day. Whenever he heard them, Raj's heart racing, he would instinctively seek out the safest place in the room, usually positioning himself near an exit or a sturdy piece of furniture. His hypervigilance had become all-consuming, making it difficult for him to relax even in the most mundane situations. Raj's self-perception had also taken a hit – he had come to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. He felt defective, unworthy of forgiveness or redemption. The event had happened because of who he was, Raj thought – a flawed individual prone to mistakes and failures. This negative self-image lingered, casting a shadow over his daily life. Despite his best efforts to move forward, Raj found himself struggling to talk about the future without becoming overwhelmed with anxiety. His grandchildren would often ask him about his plans for the upcoming holidays or family gatherings, but Raj would hesitate, unsure of how to respond. The thought of making promises or commitments filled him with a sense of trepidation – what if he failed again? What if something terrible happened? As the years went by, Raj's loved ones grew increasingly concerned about his well-being. His isolation had taken a toll on their relationships, and they encouraged him to seek professional help. It was only when Raj realized that he couldn't shake off the past on his own that he finally agreed to seek therapy – hoping against hope that he might find some measure of peace and forgiveness. Now, as Raj sat in his armchair, surrounded by the memories of a lifetime, he felt a glimmer of determination. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was willing to confront the demons that had haunted him for so long. Perhaps, with time and guidance, Raj could learn to reframe his past, to find a way to live with the memories that still lingered – and maybe, just maybe, rediscover the person he once was, before that fateful day changed everything.
